newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: The honeymoon for the new Socialist-led government continued in the French capital markets as bonds and interest rate rose after the naming of the new cabinet but many analysts said the jury was still out on whether the new grouping would ultimately be bond friendly.
Analysts said the appointment of Dominique Strauss-Kahn as finance minister caused few ripples despite Socialists plans to boost wages, cut working hours and not raise taxes.
Reports that prime minister Lionel Jospin would respect constitutional prerogatives, leaving foreign affairs in the hands of President Chirac, were also welcomed by markets.

The June future rose to a high of 129.54, helped partly by a relatively successful OAT sale which prompted some to close out hedging strategies put on earlier, but ticked lower in the afternoon with U.S. bonds amid caution ahead of a key jobs report due Friday.
The June contract settled up 0.12 at 129.26 while the spread between 10-year French and German bond yields remained unchanged at minus nine basis points.
Some analysts said they thought the Socialists would be unlikely to go back on all their policies likely to boost the French deficit and the risks of higher bond yields were real.
"At the end of day there's going to be a fiscal stimulus," Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said.
June PIBOR climbed four basis points, bringing the spread over Euromarks down to 26 from as much as 60 after the left won a surprise victory in the first round of voting on May 25.
A PIBOR trader at a French brokerage said he was perplexed by the steady rise of French interest rate futures since the left swept to power.
Some said the franc's strength against the mark, it climbed to 3.3718 on Thursday from 3.3860 after the poll result, meant the chances of any interest rate rises were almost non-existent.

Traders said the main focus besides domestic politics was the May U.S. non-farm payrolls report, due for release at 1230 GMT on Friday and expected to show a 221,000 increase in jobs after at 142,000 rise in April.
"We may see some small rallies on (politial) declarations...but honestly we waiting for (the jobs report) tomorrow," an analyst at a French brokerage said.

A sharper-than-expected rise in the number of jobs created could spark concerns the U.S. Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again which could potentially mean an increase in long-bond yields, analysts said.
There was little reaction to market talk that the Socialists would propose an EMU delay and the prime minister's office said such talk was totally unfounded.
Pierre Moscovici, French European Affairs Minister, said late on Thursday the new administration would reveal its position on the EU's stability pact to keep deficits in check.

Analysts have said the Socialists' campaign pledge to seek new talks on the stability pact, agreed last year and due to be formally approved on June 16 and 17, could be potentially destabilising for monetary union if maintained.
